title: Alignment & the Original Attention Mechanism
oneLineScope: Soft, learned alignment in neural MT (Bahdanau, Luong) — the direct ancestor of attention.
prose:
The recurrent encoder–decoder of the RNN/LSTM baseline had a structural flaw you could see coming. The encoder reads the whole source sentence and compresses it into a single fixed-width vector; the decoder then generates the translation from that one vector alone. Sutskever, Vinyals, and Le (2014) made the scheme work well enough to be startling, but it inherits the obvious liability: everything the source says must survive the squeeze through one bottleneck, no matter how long the sentence. A thirty-word clause and a four-word clause both reduce to the same number of dimensions. Empirically, translation quality held up on short inputs and then fell away as sentences grew — the tail of the source had to be remembered across many recurrent steps, through exactly the long-range degradation that doomed the recurrent models in the first place. The fixed vector is the problem; attention is the fix.

The idea: let the decoder look back

Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio (2015; the arXiv preprint is 2014) ask a simple question. Why force the decoder to work from a single summary vector when the encoder has already produced one hidden state per source word? Keep them all. At each step of decoding, let the decoder look back over the entire sequence of encoder states and assemble a fresh summary tailored to the word it is about to produce — heavy on the source positions that matter for that word, light on the rest. The paper's title says exactly what it does: it learns to align and translate jointly. There is no longer one frozen representation of the source; there is a different, content-dependent reading of the source at every output step.

This will feel familiar, because you have seen its ancestor. In the statistical machine translation you know — the IBM Models, HMM-based word alignment — an alignment is a latent variable saying which source word each target word is generated from, and you estimate a distribution over alignments by EM, as a separate model sitting beside the translation model. The E-step computes, for the current parameters, a posterior over which source word each target word came from; the M-step re-estimates the translation probabilities under that posterior; you iterate to a local optimum of the data likelihood. Attention is that same idea made differentiable and folded into the network. The alignment weights are no longer latent parameters fit by EM; they are computed on the fly from the hidden representations themselves, and gradients flow straight through them. It is soft, learned, content-addressed alignment — trained end to end by the same backpropagation that trains everything else, with no separate E-step and M-step, and no independence assumptions imposed by hand.

The distinction worth drawing sharply is where the alignment lives. In the classical pipeline the alignment is an object of inference: a distribution you compute over a discrete latent variable, with its own model and its own training procedure. In attention the alignment is a transient byproduct of a forward pass — a vector of weights that exists only for the duration of one decoding step, recomputed from scratch each time, never stored as a parameter. Nothing optimizes the alignment directly; it falls out of optimizing the translation loss, because producing a good context vector requires placing weight on the right source words. The model is rewarded for translating well, and a sensible alignment is simply what good translation needs. Hold onto this analogy; it is the most reliable way into everything that follows, and it is the reason the rest of this tutorial keeps returning to the word alignment.

Bahdanau attention, with dimensions

Fix notation. The source has length \(n\); the encoder (a bidirectional RNN in the paper) emits one hidden state per source position, \(h_j \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h}\) for \(j = 1, \ldots, n\), where \(d_h\) is the encoder's hidden width. On the decoder side we are producing target position \(i\); the decoder's own recurrent state coming into that step is \(s_{i-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_s}\), with \(d_s\) the decoder width. The mechanism is three steps.

Score. For each source position \(j\), measure how relevant \(h_j\) is to producing the next target word, given where the decoder currently stands:

\[ e_{ij} = a(s_{i-1}, h_j) = v_a^{\top} \tanh\!\left( W_s\, s_{i-1} + W_h\, h_j \right) \]

The alignment model \(a\) is a small one-hidden-layer feedforward network — the connectionist primitive you know. Here \(W_s \in \mathbb{R}^{d_a \times d_s}\) and \(W_h \in \mathbb{R}^{d_a \times d_h}\) project the two states into a shared space of width \(d_a\); \(\tanh\) is the nonlinearity; and \(v_a \in \mathbb{R}^{d_a}\) reads the result down to one scalar score \(e_{ij}\). Because the two inputs are added inside the \(\tanh\), this is called additive (or concat) attention. The matrices \(W_s, W_h, v_a\) are learned with the rest of the network.

Normalize. Turn the row of scores for output step \(i\) into a probability distribution over source positions with a softmax:

\[ \alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp(e_{ij})}{\sum_{k=1}^{n} \exp(e_{ik})}, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_{ij} = 1 \]

The \(\alpha_{ij}\) are the attention weights: nonnegative, summing to one across the source, exactly a soft alignment of target word \(i\) onto the source. This is the differentiable stand-in for the alignment posterior you would have gotten from EM — only it costs no separate inference step. The softmax does double duty here: it guarantees a valid distribution, and it is the smooth operation that keeps the whole alignment differentiable, so that nudging any score \(e_{ij}\) nudges every weight in the row in a way the chain rule can follow.

Combine. Read out a context vector as the weighted average of the encoder states:

\[ c_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_{ij}\, h_j \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{d_h} \]

Then \(c_i\) is fed into the decoder alongside \(s_{i-1}\) and the previous output to produce target word \(i\). Note what has changed: \(c_i\) is recomputed at every output step, so the source summary the decoder sees is never frozen. Where the seq2seq decoder worked from one summary for the whole sentence, this decoder gets a private, freshly assembled summary for each word it emits — and crucially, because \(c_i\) is a direct weighted sum of the encoder states, the gradient from the loss reaches any source position in a single hop, with no decay along a long recurrent chain. That short path is exactly what the fixed-vector bottleneck denied.

Stack the weight rows for all target positions and you get a matrix \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times n}\) (with \(T\) the target length) — the soft alignment matrix, learned end to end. Plot it and you see the model has discovered, with no alignment supervision, that the words line up roughly monotonically with the expected local reorderings around them. It is the same object an IBM model would give you, drawn as the same heatmap, but it was never trained to produce it. That picture — a sensible alignment emerging for free from a translation objective — is the payoff of the whole approach, and the diagram below shows one such matrix for a short French-to-English example.

Luong: global vs. local, and the multiplicative shortcut

Luong, Pham, and Manning (2015) tidied the idea and, importantly for us, changed the scoring function. They distinguish global attention, which attends over all source positions as above, from local attention, which first predicts a position to focus near and attends only within a small window — cheaper, and a deliberate echo of the hard-alignment habit of classical MT. Their lasting contribution, though, is a family of simpler scoring functions that drop Bahdanau's extra feedforward layer:

\[ \text{dot:}\quad e_{ij} = s_i^{\top} h_j, \qquad \text{general:}\quad e_{ij} = s_i^{\top} W_a\, h_j \]

The dot form is just the inner product of the two states — a direct measure of compatibility in their shared space, with no parameters at all. The general form inserts one learned matrix \(W_a \in \mathbb{R}^{d_s \times d_h}\) to align the spaces first (and to handle the case \(d_s \neq d_h\), where a bare inner product would not even be defined). These are multiplicative scores, and the dot-product form is the conceptual hinge of this whole tutorial: replace the small feedforward alignment net with a single inner product, and you are one short step from the \(QK^{\top}\) at the center of scaled dot-product attention. The trade is the usual one. Additive scoring runs every query–state pair through a nonlinearity, which can express richer compatibility but must be evaluated pair by pair; the dot product collapses to a single matrix multiply over all pairs at once, which a GPU devours, at the cost of that extra expressive layer. Luong's experiments found the two competitive in quality, and on modern hardware the speed of the multiplicative form is decisive — which is why the architecture that took over chose it.

Where it connects

What you have here is cross-attention: the queries come from the decoder, the keys and values from the encoder, and the alignment runs between two different sequences — precisely the soft, learned successor to IBM-style word alignment. The next node makes two moves on top of this. First, it has a sequence attend to itself — queries, keys, and values all projected from the same input — which is self-attention. Second, it factors the operation cleanly into three learned projections \(W_Q, W_K, W_V\) producing queries, keys, and values, scores them by dot product (Luong's form, now between projected vectors), and divides by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) to keep the softmax responsive as the dimension grows. The soft-alignment idea is identical to what you have just seen; scaled dot-product attention simply industrializes it and turns it inward.

diagrams.caption: One decoder step of Bahdanau attention: score each encoder state, softmax to weights, then take the weighted sum as the context vector.
diagrams.altText: A diagram for decoder step i. On the left, a column of encoder hidden states h_1, h_2, h_3, ellipsis, h_T, each in the real numbers to the d. The previous decoder state s_{i-1} sits below an alignment net box a, labeled e = vᵀ tanh(W h + U s). Each encoder state and s_{i-1} feed the alignment net, producing T scalar scores e_{ij}. The scores pass into a softmax over j = 1..T producing attention weights alpha_{ij} that satisfy sum over j of alpha_{ij} = 1. The weights and the same encoder states (the values being mixed) feed a weighted-sum node, producing the context vector c_i in the real numbers to the d, which is fed to the decoder at step i.

On the left, a column of encoder hidden state boxes labeled 'h_1', 'h_2', 'h_3', a vertical ellipsis, and 'h_T', annotated 'each h_j ∈ ℝ^d'. A box labeled 'a' titled 'alignment net' carries the formula 'e = vᵀ tanh(W h + U s)'. Below it, a box for the previous decoder state labeled 's_(i−1)'. Arrows from each encoder state and from s_(i−1) feed the alignment net, producing a box of scores labeled 'e_ij' annotated 'T scalars'. An arrow leads to a 'softmax' box annotated 'over j = 1..T' and 'Σ_j α_ij = 1', producing a weights box labeled 'α_ij' annotated 'T weights'. The weights feed a summation node labeled 'Σ' ('weighted sum of h_j'); the same encoder states h_1..h_T are also routed into the sum as the values being mixed. The sum produces a context vector box labeled 'c_i' annotated 'context, ∈ ℝ^d' and '→ fed to decoder step i'. Emphasize the scores, weights, and context vector as the heart of the step. Label every element. Structural diagram: flow and labels must be exact.

diagrams.caption: A learned soft-alignment matrix: French source words across the columns, English target words down the rows, each cell shaded by its attention weight α — the differentiable cousin of an IBM-model alignment.
diagrams.altText: A grid with French source words on the columns (L', accord, sur, la, zone) and English target words down the rows (The, agreement, on, the, area). Each cell is shaded by the attention weight alpha_ij: darker means stronger alignment. Most weight lies on a near-diagonal path, with the last two rows ('the', 'area') showing a small reordering around 'la' and 'zone'. Notes explain that darker cells mean larger alpha, each target row sums to one, and this is the soft analogue of IBM-model or HMM word alignment but learned by gradient descent rather than EM.

Make the shading show a near-diagonal alignment: 'The'→'L'', 'agreement'→'accord', 'on'→'sur', then the last two rows show a small reordering where 'the' spreads across 'la'/'zone' and 'area' aligns strongly to 'zone'. Add margin notes: 'darker cell = larger α_ij (stronger alignment)'; 'each target row sums to 1 — a soft distribution over source words'; and, tying to the reader's background, 'cf. bibliography.citation: Bahdanau, D., Cho, K., & Bengio, Y. (2015). "Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate." ICLR.
bibliography.annotation: The origin of attention. §3 defines the additive alignment model a(s,h) = vᵀ tanh(W_s s + W_h h), the softmax weights, and the context vector; §6.3 shows the learned soft-alignment matrices that motivate the whole construction. Read it for the original framing of alignment as a differentiable, jointly-trained alternative to a separate latent-variable model.

bibliography.citation: Luong, M.-T., Pham, H., & Manning, C. D. (2015). "Effective Approaches to Attention-based Neural Machine Translation." EMNLP.
bibliography.annotation: Introduces global vs. local attention and the multiplicative scoring functions — dot (sᵀh) and general (sᵀ W h) — in §3. The dot-product score here is the direct conceptual precursor to the QKᵀ of scaled dot-product attention; read §3.1 for the scoring comparison.

bibliography.citation: Sutskever, I., Vinyals, O., & Le, Q. V. (2014). "Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks." NeurIPS.
bibliography.annotation: The fixed-vector encoder–decoder that attention was invented to fix. Read §1–§3 for the bottleneck this node opens with; their own reversed-input trick is a tell that the single summary vector strains on long sentences.

bibliography.citation: Zhang, A., Lipton, Z. C., Li, M., & Smola, A. J. "Dive into Deep Learning" — Attention Mechanisms chapter.
bibliography.annotation: A clean, code-backed walk from the seq2seq bottleneck through Bahdanau attention to scoring functions, with runnable examples and the alignment-heatmap visualizations. The best place to see the matrices and shapes worked end to end before moving on to self-attention.
